title: Putting the Pro in Prom Photo Poses
summary: Prom poses for solo, couple and group photos: what to do in a gown or a suit, corsage shots, and poses that survive a driveway at five o'clock.
body_markdown:
## Catching the perfect moments before prom night


*Angle the hips, link the arms, and even a row of four stops reading as a lineup.*


A prom photoshoot does not happen at prom. It happens on a front lawn at five in the afternoon, with four sets of parents, a car nobody is allowed to lean on, and a sun sitting high enough for a full length shoot.


‍


That is the real assignment, and it is a good one. Forty minutes, a driveway, and a group of people who have never looked better and know it.


‍


The constraints are what make it straightforward. Get off the square-on standing shot, keep everyone moving, and put the light behind you. Everything below follows from those three.


## Solo poses in a gown or a suit


*Body angled away, face turned back. The turn still works once the skirt has settled.*


Start with the turn. In a long gown, walk two steps and pivot, and let the skirt keep moving. The frame that works is the one taken half a beat later.


Then sit on something. Front steps are the best furniture available: one knee higher than the other, skirt forward, a forearm on the raised knee. Seated poses give your arms an easy job.


The over-shoulder is the third. Turn your back three-quarters to the camera and look back over the shoulder closest to the lens. In a backless or detailed dress this is the frame that shows off the dress.


In a suit: hands in pockets with the thumbs out, one foot crossed over the other in a lean, or a jacket-button adjustment caught mid-motion.


## Couple poses that are not a school-dance sway


*His hand at her waist, hers thrown open. A back hug does not have to hold still.*


Left to themselves, most couples land in the same spot: side by side, arms straight down, smiling at whichever parent is closest. It is a fine instinct. It just runs out after one frame.


So give them something to do. The walk is easiest: hold hands and cross the lawn while talking, and keep shooting through it. Nobody holds a stiff face while actually walking and talking.


The back hug is the reliable one. He stands behind her, arms around her waist, her hands over his, both chins turned toward the light. It sorts out a height difference on its own because the contact point sits low.


The forehead touch works for the same reason. Faces angled in, foreheads together, eyes closed, hands anywhere comfortable. It photographs as closeness rather than as posing.


Where there is a big height gap, put her on a step above him rather than asking anyone to bend, because bending shows.


## Corsage and boutonnière shots worth taking


*Both flowers in one frame. Shoot the corsage going on and the boutonnière comes free.*


The first is the pinning or the slipping-on, shot over a shoulder with the hands and the flower sharp and the faces soft behind. It happens exactly once, so be ready for it.


The second is a tight detail: a wrist with the corsage against the gown, or a lapel with the boutonnière. Shoot close and let the background go to nothing.


## Friend and group poses that fit everyone in


*Arms behind backs, everyone leaning in. That is what stops a row reading as a row.*


Eight friends in a straight line is a lineup, and it is the easiest thing in the world to improve. Stagger it so half the group steps forward a pace, giving the frame front and back rather than one flat row, and alternate heights so faces are not all at the same level.


For larger groups, get elevation. Shooting from three or four steps up shows every face instead of the back of the front row.


Take two versions: one organised frame for the parents, and one where you tell them to talk to each other and ignore you. The second is the one that gets posted. Keep any frame under about eight people, since beyond that faces get too small to read on a phone.


## Working with a driveway at five o'clock


A high afternoon sun is the one thing worth planning around, and there are two good ways to do it.


Put the sun behind the group. You get a rim of light on hair and shoulders, everyone can open their eyes, and faces are lit by soft bounce off the driveway and the house.


If that is impossible, find shade with an open view. The strip of shadow along the side of a house works well, and so does a tree, as long as dappled light is not landing on faces.


There is more in our breakdown of[the best and worst options for outdoor photo light](https://www.snappr.com/blog/what-are-your-best-and-worst-options-to-get-the-best-light-for-your-outdoor-photos) . And if you are weighing up whether to hire someone rather than handing a phone to a parent, our notes on[getting the most out of a party photographer](https://www.snappr.com/blog/4-tips-to-getting-the-most-out-of-a-holiday-party-photographer) apply almost exactly.

## Frequently asked questions


### What are the best prom poses for couples?


The walk, the back hug and the forehead touch cover most of a session. All three use movement or contact rather than a held position, and the last two solve height differences on their own because contact happens below shoulder height.


### How do I pose in a prom dress?


Turn rather than face forward. Walk two steps and pivot so the skirt keeps moving, look back over the shoulder nearest the camera to show the back of the dress, and sit on steps with one knee raised to give your arms somewhere to rest.


### What should I do with my hands in prom photos?


Give them contact or a task. In a couple frame, hands go on a waist, over another set of hands, or linked while walking. Solo, rest a forearm on a raised knee, hold a clutch low to one side, or use pockets with thumbs out in a suit.


### What time should prom photos be taken?


As late as the schedule allows, with the sun behind you rather than in front. If photos have to happen under a high afternoon sun, move into even shade along the side of a house instead of standing on an open lawn.
